items.originalTitle: Poll: Midterm losses deepen divide between MAGA and non-MAGA Trump voters
items.author: Erin Doherty
items.title: Poll: Midterm losses deepen divide between MAGA and non-MAGA Trump voters
items.summary: The Republican Party’s midterm wipeout has torn apart President Donald Trump’s coalition. For months, polling has shown cracks among Trump’s 2024 voters over immigration , the Iran war and the president’s influence. Now, new results from The POLITICO Poll , conducted just days after the election, reveal a deep chasm between Trump’s self-identified MAGA base and the non-MAGA voters who helped fuel his return to the White House. The two camps hold sharply different interpretations of the GOP’s historic midterm defeat and what comes next for their party, according to the survey conducted by PF Global. MAGA Trump loyalists were more likely to say the president is not to blame for the losses — that things would have gone better if he was on the ballot — and that the party should now move closer to Trump. Non-MAGA Trump voters starkly disagreed, saying they are ready to move away from him and his unpopular agenda. About one in five said they voted for Democratic candidates this cycle. The fault line is a fresh warning sign that Republicans, desperate to stitch back together a winning coalition after their midterm calamity, may struggle to keep the voters that powered Trump’s victory in 2024 in the fold. And it calls into question just how loyal the party should be to a leader — and movement — it has spent the last decade united around. Overall, just over half of all Trump voters said the president will be able to make a comeback from the election losses. “As the [GOP] spends the next two years figuring out who it is and what it stands for, these divisions will only be further exposed,” said Republican strategist Doug Heye. Here are four charts that show just how much the midterms have divided Trump’s own voters. A majority of non-MAGA Trump voters blamed Republicans' loss of the House and the Senate on Trump’s actions since taking office, with far fewer saying the campaigns themselves were responsible. A 59% majority also said the president is a loser of the midterms, a striking rebuke from a group of voters who helped his return to the White House. But MAGA Trump voters are torn over who they blame for their losses. The divide mirrors disagreements happening at the top levels of the Republican Party. In the immediate aftermath of the election, some Republicans, at least tepidly, began pointing fingers at the president. Others have called for a “reckoning” without explicitly laying the blame at Trump’s feet or articulating an alternative vision for the GOP. “There is no way to sugarcoat what happened on Election Day. From coast to coast, and in some of the reddest parts of the country, Republicans were humiliated,” 31 Republican National Committee members wrote in a letter to GOP lawmakers this week. Trump, who ahead of the midterms repeatedly urged voters to “pretend” he was on the ballot, insisted in a Truth Social post after the election that, “I JUST WASN’T ON THE BALLOT. IF I WERE, WE WOULD HAVE WON IN A LANDSLIDE!” “President Trump will never stop delivering results for the American people and he will undoubtedly go down as the most successful and consequential president in American history,” White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said in a statement. As Republican Party leaders grapple with how to rebound from the midterms, MAGA isn’t ready to move on from Trump: They said the path forward is embracing Trump and his agenda. Non-MAGA Trump voters said the opposite — and nearly half of them think their Republican candidates should have broken with the president on the economy this cycle. “It is very clear that Election Day 2026 was an unequivocal rebuke of Donald Trump, both him personally and his policies,” said one national GOP operative who worked on midterm races, granted anonymity to speak candidly about the landscape. “MAGA needs a serious rebrand if it is going to have any success in the future.” That presents a complicated picture for Republican leaders, who will have to find a way to appeal to Trump’s fiercely loyal MAGA base without alienating the less committed voters who helped deliver his 2024 victory. On Election Night, as the scale of Republican losses was becoming clear, POLITICO asked GOP operatives who worked on midterm races whether the defeat meant it was time for Republicans to consider a new vision for the party. “How can it not be?” one person responded. It’s “the worst defeat a party has taken in 50 years.” Non-MAGA Trump voters are split over whether Trump can make a comeback after the midterms bloodbath. MAGA, however, is quite confident in the president’s abilities to do so. And collectively, Trump voters are more optimistic about the Republican Party than the president. Some key aspects of Trump’s agenda are unpopular with Americans, including his push for mass deportations, tariffs imposed on key trade partners and the war in Iran. The congressional Republicans who once supported many of those policies are now weighing whether they can distance themselves to regain voters’ trust. In an interview with “ 60 Minutes ” after the midterms, Trump admitted his party’s losses may be attributed at least in part to the Iran war and the resulting high gas prices — though he also mentioned how, in some cases, voters “didn’t like the candidates” and asserted, again, that he wasn’t on the ballot. "President Trump remains the unequivocal leader of our party who's cut taxes, lowered drug costs and secured our border,” RNC spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre said in a statement. “Republicans will continue to harness his ability to energize our base and expose the Democrats' disastrous record to win back our majorities in 2028." As the party looks ahead to 2028, Republicans are already weighing how much the party’s next presidential nominee should carry the MAGA mantle. Some Hill Republicans are increasingly warming to the prospect of a Marco Rubio presidential bid, arguing that voters may be looking for a new direction after Trump — and Vice President JD Vance may be too closely tied to the president’s agenda. MAGA Trump voters said decisively that they prefer someone who has worked in the administration — another sign of their support for the president, and of the difficulty of changing course as a party given that loyalty. “I think everybody reserves the right to adjust. You know, learn from this,” GOP Rep. and incoming Oklahoma Sen. Kevin Hern recently told POLITICO . Asked his favorite candidate of the three he expected to run: Vance, Rubio or DeSantis, he replied with a smile: “Everybody.”

Among them is the Fanttik S1 Pro Cordless Electric Screwdriver , which is currently matching its all-time low of $39.99 ($40 off) at Amazon for a limited time. Fanttik S1 Pro Cordless Electric Screwdriver Where to Buy: $79.99 $39.99 at Amazon $79.99 $45.99 at Fanttik Fanttik’s rechargeable tool is designed to make everyday household repairs and DIY projects easier, and it does a good job. Verge commerce editor Brandon Widder once called it his go-to electric screwdriver, noting he’s used it to assemble a bed, tighten bike seats, and perform other small- to medium-sized tasks around the house. It offers three adjustable torque settings, so you can use a gentler setting for more delicate jobs like electronics and more power for tougher projects. Beyond being a capable electric screwdriver, the Fanttik also comes equipped with a few extra conveniences. For example, it features a built-in LED light to help you see screws in darker spaces, such as under a desk or inside a cabinet. The screwdriver also comes with 16 S2 hardened steel bits, including flathead and Torx bits, all of which fit inside an included magnetic storage case. The rechargeable 2,000mAh battery should handle up to 340 screws on a single charge, too, and it supports USB-C so you can quickly charge it between projects.

items.title: LG’s budget-friendly B6E OLED TV is up to 50 percent off this weekend
items.summary: LG’s B6E was already one of the most affordable OLED TVs you could buy, but it’s an even better deal now that it’s included as part of Best Buy’s latest doorbuster event. Now through the end of today, November 15th, the 55-inch model is 50 percent off, dropping it to an all-time low of $699.99 ($700 off) at Best Buy . If you want a larger 4K set, the 65- and 77-inch models are also discounted, dropping them to $999.99 ($900 off) and $1,499.99 ($1,200 off) , respectively. LG B6E OLED TV Where to Buy: $1399.99 $699.99 at Best Buy (55-inch) $1899.99 $999.99 at Best Buy (65-inch) $2699.99 $1499.99 at Best Buy (77-inch) Although it’s not as bright as LG’s pricier C6 , the B6E still delivers the excellent contrast and deep blacks OLEDs are often praised for. It’s nearly identical to the standard B6, except it comes with a simpler remote that lacks the motion controls and voice features found on LG’s Magic Remote. It supports Dolby Vision and HDR10 for more lifelike colors and detail in bright and dark scenes, along with Dolby Atmos for more immersive audio. And with Apple AirPlay and Google Cast built in, you can easily stream content from your phone or tablet and access a variety of streaming apps, including Netflix, HBO Max, and YouTube via LG’s webOS platform. The B6 also offers a lot of features gamers will appreciate. It has a 120Hz refresh rate for modern gaming consoles, which is still plenty fast even if it doesn’t rival the 165Hz refresh rate on the C6. It also offers variable refresh rate support — including Nvidia G-Sync and AMD FreeSync Premium — to help minimize screen tearing. You also get a zippy Alpha 8 Gen 3 AI processor and four HDMI 2.1 ports, making it easy to connect multiple consoles. It may lack some of the more advanced features found on LG’s more premium OLED TVs, but at 50 percent off, the B6 is a great option if you want the benefits of OLED without spending a fortune.

items.originalTitle: Kindness of strangers: I was stranded, dressed as a flapper, on a freezing night. Then a cheerful taxi driver pulled over
items.author: Carole Edmunds as told to Katie Cunningham
items.title: Kindness of strangers: I was stranded, dressed as a flapper, on a freezing night. Then a cheerful taxi driver pulled over
items.summary: My tyre was blown so he changed it for me. When I offered payment, he said ‘Don’t be ridiculous love’ Read more in the kindness of strangers series I had to fight not to lose control of the car. I was in my early 20s and driving home from a fancy dress party when bang – my tyre suddenly blew. I managed to wrestle my Toyota Corolla to a stop without crashing and sat there, heart pounding, as I wondered what to do next. It was 1982 in Canberra; a foggy, bitterly cold night in the middle of winter. I was wearing a silly flapper dress and high heels – I’m not sure I’d even packed a jacket! I had a spare tyre in the back, but little idea how to change it. My options were to make the one hour walk home alone or wait to see if another car passed and could offer me a ride. For 30 minutes I sat in the driver’s seat helplessly, unsure what to do.

items.author: Shadi Khan Saif
items.title: How do we face uncertainty without allowing it to overwhelm us? This Islamic teaching shows us the way
items.summary: For generations of Muslims, tawakkul has been an essential part of faith – making a sincere effort while recognising the limits of human control I once asked an elderly naan seller on the streets of Kabul how he was managing to make a living. It was almost midday and he had not sold a single naan. What would he take home, I asked. “ Tawakkul ba Khuda, ” he replied. He had a long silver beard, deep brown eyes and a beautiful smile. As a frontline journalist covering the Afghan war, I had heard those words many times before. From a young woman trying to establish a clothing business in the middle of the conflict, to a military commander confronting a deadly insurgency, to a school student preparing for the long and uncertain journey towards a university degree, the expression seemed to surface wherever hope and hardship met.

items.originalTitle: All Hail Philomena Cunk, the Perfect Fake Newswoman for Our Age of Ignorance
items.author: Judy Berman
items.title: All Hail Philomena Cunk, the Perfect Fake Newswoman for Our Age of Ignorance
items.summary: Diane Morgan in Cunk on Cinema —Netflix In the future, when some documentary series in whatever medium succeeds television looks back at the current decade in public discourse, it might name our era the Age of Ignorance. The crank shouting nonsense from atop a soapbox is, of course, nothing new. What’s unique to our time is how vast the audiences for these bloviators have become. We’ve got Alix Earle , with about 15 million followers across TikTok and Instagram, bragging about never having read a book. (Even if it wasn’t strictly true, how telling that she would let us believe it.) We’ve got Joe Rogan , by many measures the most popular podcaster out there—a guy who has platformed pandemic misinformation and had to apologize for using racial slurs — influencing nationwide elections . Just last week , Fox News star turned YouTuber Tucker Carlson entertained the possibility that the Smithsonian is suppressing evidence of the existence of Goliath-like giants. To which Philomena Cunk says: “Hold my snake oil.” The world-famous British TV presenter described by the Guardian as “ iconically stupid ” is back on Netflix and BBC Two with Cunk on Cinema , a six-part docuseries in which she gripes that reading subtitles makes it impossible to concentrate on one’s phone and pronounces D.W. Griffith’s KKK mash note The Birth of a Nation a “typically woke Hollywood fantasy.” (In what may or may not be a nod to viewers’ short attention spans, episodes top out at 15 minutes and can be binged in less time than it takes to watch most films.) Cunk is so incompetent, it’s hilarious. But unlike the personalities listed above, she’s meant to be funny—because she is a fictional character played by Diane Morgan. And although she was conceived when Earle was a tween and Carlson had bosses to answer to, she has since become the perfect fake newswoman to send up our Age of Ignorance. She may not be a real human being, but Cunk has had the kind of rise broadcast journalists dream about. After making her name in 2013 as an astonishingly dim yet opinionated commentator on Black Mirror creator Charlie Brooker ’s BBC Two comedy news show Weekly Wipe , she leveled up to hosting mockumentaries like Cunk on Shakespeare and Cunk on Britain , all helmed by Brooker. Like the other thought leaders we trust to guide us through complex topics on screen, in her solo efforts, Cunk combines her own explanations and analyses (“If the Tudors were the Kardashians of their time, this was their Kim: Henry of Eight”) with real expert interviews. “How important are the words in a Shakespeares [sic] play?” she once asked the venerable Shakespearean actor Simon Russell Beale. “Could you do it without the words?” In early 2023, she broke UK containment, arriving on Netflix with her own, let’s say, unique, series-length take on world history, Cunk on Earth . Two years later, her special Cunk on Life dared to ask big questions about nature and the universe—the implicit one being: What would Planet Earth be like if Sir David Attenborough had the intellect of a microorganism? Diane Morgan in Cunk on Cinema —Netflix Philomena Cunk is a very British creation, in the tradition of Steve Coogan’s boorish TV-presenter character Alan Partridge and Sacha Baron Cohen ’s Da Ali G Show alter egos. From SNL ’s “Weekend Update” to The Daily Show , America’s news-satire tradition favors comedians telling dark jokes about current events in their own voices. But by the time she crossed the Atlantic, three years ago, U.S. audiences were primed to make Cunk a cult-comedy hero stateside, circulating her quotes and searching YouTube for morsels of her earlier work. Cunk on Life even scored a pair of Emmy nominations . It’s true that Baron Cohen broke out bigger in the U.S., during the 2000s, especially with his ingenuously inappropriate Kazakh reporter character, Borat. But his heyday coincided with a golden age of confrontational political satire, when Michael Moore broke box office records with documentaries built around interviews that embarrassed conservative icons like Charlton Heston and culture jammers like the Yes Men captured their elaborate anti-corporate hoaxes in feature films. Baron Cohen did something similar. As Baron Cohen wrote in an essay for TIME that coincided with the October release of his feature Ali G: Who Iz I? : “Each of my characters has a specific mechanism to encourage people to drop their guards and show what they really believe, prejudices and all.” In one notorious Ali G Show stunt, Borat got the patrons of an Arizona honky-tonk singing and clapping along to a song about throwing Jews down a well (though some later said they were behaving as directed or always knew it was all a bit). Morgan has a different agenda. She rarely humiliates the experts she interviews, who are generally in on the joke but, as in real news programs, aren’t given the questions in advance. Sure, she does occasionally mystify someone. In Cunk on Cinema , that person is Michael Bay , who at one point exclaims: “These are odd questions!” Most of the time, Cunk only embarrasses herself, though she’s too dim to realize it. The cringe comedy comes from the way the character makes the leading minds in every field behave as though the idiotic non sequiturs she imposes on them are worth engaging with. They’re too polite (or leery of coming off as elitists) not to. And when they do ever-so-gently push back, she tends to perform offendedness. “What was the Soviet Onion?” she asks a history professor in Cunk on Earth . She must mean the Soviet Union, he replies. “I don’t wanna be rude,” Cunk counters, despite much evidence to the contrary, “but I think you’re mansplaining a bit.” As Brooker has said : “The strange thing about Cunk is she’s sort of weirdly in charge of things, even if she’s speaking to a professor or whatever.” Diane Morgan in Cunk on Cinema —Netflix Between interviews, she pontificates in the tones of a veteran newsreader, albeit one who has no understanding of the subject on which she’s been asked to extemporize. Cunk on Cinema will be extra entertaining to anyone who’s ever read a book or taken a survey course on the history of film, because of how deftly it plays on the field’s tropes and touchstones. Stanley Kubrick ca. 2001: A Space Odyssey is described offhandedly as a “groovy young director.” She refers to Soviet montage master Sergei Eisenstein’s landmark silent film Battleship Potemkin as Batsh-t Pumpkin , “one of cinema’s unwatchable masterpieces.” You needn’t have a Ph.D in Cinema Studies to appreciate the humor Brooker and Morgan wring out of Cunk’s hopelessness with names and titles. Wayne John, Marlo Brandon, E Dot T Dot (a.k.a. E.T. ). Quentin Tarantino , she informs us, “is Italian for five spiders.” If you’ve ever listened to a TikToker with no medical training evangelize unregulated peptide injections, you’ll see mirrored in Cunk the blithe confidence of a person who’s getting rich repackaging their ignorance as subversive truth-telling. When she wonders, “Was James Dean born a teenager?,” it’s a benign version of the level of question we typically get from podcast hosts who spend three-hour episodes credulously “hearing out” conspiracy theorists. Now, as you might expect from a writing team led by the Black Mirror guy, she’s got artificial intelligence to hallucinate along with her. In Cunk on Cinema , she insists to Die Hard screenwriter Steven E. de Souza that the all-American genius of silent comedy Buster Keaton spoke in a Cornish accent, then plays him the AI audio to “prove” it. I don’t want to minimize the brilliance of Morgan’s deadpan performance or Brooker’s jokes, which approach the linguistic density of poetry and tend to contain sneaky insights that would be lost on the character giving voice to them. ( Marilyn Monroe , says Cunk, “effortlessly blended sex appeal, vulnerability, comic timing, and innocence into one irresistible package for men to destroy.”) Yet I suspect so many of us love to laugh at Cunk because, for once in this choose-your-own-facts decade, the joke is on the fool or cynic with outsize influence instead of on anyone fed up with the latter contingent’s misinformation and glibness and idiocy and self-promotion at any cost. There’s a difference between thoughtful questions and thoughtless ones, informed opinions and hysterical polemic, challenging authority on principle and mindless contrarianism for personal gain. And it’s a relief to be reminded that someone still knows it.

items.originalTitle: Caravaggio
items.author: Pietro Bucciarelli / Connected Archives
items.title: Caravaggio
items.summary: Teach me how to circumvent Wall Street at noon when the facades are dark and the sky is platinum. Teach me how the apple eats the worm and the woman and man disappear into air and gold leaf. Teach me how the folds of a robe shake out the moths of light and the black sand of the desert. Teach me Judith, Bacchus, Medusa, heroes of anathema, lovers of the lowlands. What stares at me now in the growing dark? The head of Holofernes or the red cloth above his face?

items.originalTitle: Why would anyone want a smart fridge? | Dave Schilling
items.author: Dave Schilling
items.title: Why would anyone want a smart fridge? | Dave Schilling
items.summary: After a hack in France, internet-enabled appliances are looking even less appealing – especially before the holidays We are deep into the holiday season now, past Halloween and a mere two weeks away from American Thanksgiving. I’ve already given up taking care of my body, surrendering fully to gluttony, vices, and going to bed at 7pm because it’s pitch black outside. I’ve begun to hibernate like a slothful bear, my blanket and pillow never too far from my grasp. The only thing closer to my hands than my bedsheets is a slice of cold pizza. I just want to eat in peace, thank you very much.

items.title: Our five-year-old has hearing loss and may one day be blind. Here is where I find hope
items.summary: Ali Stevens’ daughter was a baby when they discovered she has a syndrome which causes deafblindness. There’s no roadmap for change – but what gets her through is the same as for any parent My daughter Poppy is five. She’s energetic and curious, loves dresses, books and creating new things and spends a lot of time playing with her big sister, Evie. When Poppy was born, my husband, Ben, and I were focused on the usual joys of welcoming a new baby. A routine hearing screening showed something wasn’t quite right, although initially we were told it was probably fluid in her ears.

items.originalTitle: Gout is on the rise – and excruciating. Why are sufferers still judged for it?
items.author: Tim Dowling
items.title: Gout is on the rise – and excruciating. Why are sufferers still judged for it?
items.summary: About 1.6 million people in the UK have this agonising condition, but it is often viewed as a comical malady brought on by overconsumption and idleness. What can be done to end the stigma? Brett McAllister-Byrne was in his early 30s when he first noticed a sharp ache in his ankle and big toe. “I felt it the night after playing football, and I thought I must have had a knock or something,” he says. “But then it just got worse and worse.” The next morning McAllister-Byrne, an urban planner, was in too much pain to go to work. When he described the episode to his family, they suggested it might be gout. “I was like, really?” he says. “Can you get that in your 30s?”
